## Introduction to the Text

(a) Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, I shall speak the Khuddasikkhā, which includes the matrix (mātikā) and should be studied from the beginning of one's ordination.

In this Khuddasikkhā, this is the matrix:

(b) The four Pārājikas, the nine Garuka offenses (Saṅghādisesa), robes, dyes, the bowl, serving dishes, and the refusal of further food (pavāraṇā).

(c) The periods for consumption (kālika), the formal acceptance (paṭiggāha), unallowable meats, the Nissaggiya objects, the pure Pācittiyas, the methods of making allowable (kappiya) for monks, and the allowable grounds (kappiyabhūmi).

(d) The duties toward the preceptor (upajjhāya) and the teacher (ācariya), the duties to be performed at the place of easing nature, the duties of asking permission, the duties of monks without clothing, the allowable bathing, and those who should not be paid homage.

(e) Hides, sandals, objects that should not be looked at, the collyrium tube, unallowable beds and seats, and those with whom one shares a seat.

(f) Those with whom one should not associate, formal acts (kamma), abstaining from wrong livelihood, duties (vatta), the method of making over (vikappanā), the taking of dependence (nissaya), and the waist-band.

## 1. Exposition of the Pārājikas

Regarding the words "The four Pārājikas":
If a monk who has not renounced the training inserts his sexual organ, even as much as a sesame seed, into the three paths (the anus, the urethra, or the mouth), whether covered or uncovered, or in a moist place, whether covered or uncovered, he falls from the Sasana.

Alternatively, in a case where he is forced by others, if he consents at the moment of entry, the moment of remaining, the moment of withdrawal, or the moment after entry, he also falls from the Sasana.

If a monk who has not renounced the training takes by way of a lawsuit with the intention to steal property not given by the owner; or if he takes it with the intention to steal while carrying it away; or if he takes property deposited with him without returning it; or if he causes the owner's posture or the living property's posture to change; or if he moves it from its place; or if he passes the designated customs post.

If that monk takes property not given by the owner with the intention to steal, he becomes one who has fallen into Pārājika. Alternatively, he becomes Pārājika through stealing by concealment and deception, by force, by changing a label or mark, by covering with dust or leaves etc., or by plotting for the location of the goods. In this Adinnādāna, the decision must be made based on the goods, the time, the value, the location, and the usage.

If he, aiming at a human body, deprives it of life; or if, with the intention to cause death, he places a weapon for that person.
133:
If he causes one to take up a means of death, or if he speaks of the benefits of death. If death occurs due to efforts such as killing by oneself, killing by throwing, killing by command, or killing by permanent means (such as a trap), he falls into Pārājika.

There is also killing by psychic power and killing by magical arts. These six: time, object/person, weapon, posture, specific action, and location, are the markers of a command (āṇatti).

If one claims for oneself superior human states (uttarimanussadhamma) such as Jhāna etc., which are not present in oneself, whether claiming them individually or as a group, and basing it on the present life;

Without referring to another, and not being one who is under a delusion, if he makes it known through the path of intimation by body or by speech, and if it is understood by the listener, he falls into Pārājika.

These four Pārājikas are without association as before. Just as a man with his head cut off is unable to live, so they are no longer fit for the state of a monk.

In the third Pārājika, both indirect means (pariyāya) and command (āṇatti) are obtained. In the second Pārājika, however, only command is obtained. In the remaining two (the first and fourth), neither of these two is obtained.

The mind desiring to indulge and the insertion of the organ into a path—these two, the wise say, are the factors of the act of sexual intercourse (methunadhamma).
134: The property belonging to a human, the perception of that property as belonging to a human, the intention to steal, the object being of heavy value worth one pāda or more than one pāda, and the act of stealing—these five are the factors for the taking of what is not given (the second Pārājika). Being a human being, the perception of it as a living being, the intention to kill, the effort to kill, and death because of that effort—these five are the factors for killing (the third Pārājika). The superior human state not being present in oneself, speaking with evil desire, the person spoken to being a human, speaking directly of oneself without referring to another, and the listener understanding at the very moment of speaking—these five are the factors for the manifestation of non-existent superior human states (the fourth Pārājika). The four uncommon Pārājikas of bhikkhunīs which do not apply to bhikkhus, the eleven types of disqualified persons (abhabba), a bhikkhunī who has returned to the lay life, a monk with a flexible back who inserts his organ into his own mouth or anus, a monk with a long organ who inserts it into his own mouth or anus, a monk who takes another's organ with his mouth, and a monk who sits down by pressing upon another's organ—these four are the derivative (anulomika) Pārājikas corresponding to the Pārājika of sexual intercourse. There are also four Pārājikas directly mentioned in this Khuddasikkhā text regarding the act of sexual intercourse, namely the insertion of the organ into a path. Thus, when all are combined, there are 24 Pārājikas.

## 2. Saᅅghādisesaniddeso

The nine grave offenses are:

Except for the case of a dream, a monk who makes an effort with the intention to emit semen and causes it to be emitted, falls into a grave offense.

Perceiving a human woman as a woman, a monk with lustful intent for physical contact who makes an effort and touches her, falls into a grave offense.

Likewise, a monk who, with lustful desire for lewd speech, speaks wickedly to a woman who is capable of understanding and hearing, concerning the genital organs or sexual intercourse, falls into a grave offense.

A monk with lustful desire for sexual intercourse who speaks in praise of the merit of serving him with sexual intercourse, or who requests sexual intercourse with words connected to sexual intercourse, falls into a grave offense.

A monk who accepts a message (matchmaking) from a woman or a man, and after inquiring, carries the message back and speaks it, falls into a grave offense.

A monk who builds a small hut for himself, using materials he himself has begged for, on a site not designated by the Saᅅgha, and which exceeds the prescribed measurements, falls into a grave offense.

A monk who builds a large monastery for his own residence on a site not designated by the Saᅅgha, falls into a grave offense.

A monk who, with the intention of causing another to fall from the Sasana, accuses him or causes another to accuse him of a groundless Pārājika offense, falls into a grave offense if there is a person present to hear it.
136:
A monk who, seeing the actions (such as sexual intercourse) of another (Kshatriya) man, and using that as a mere pretext, accuses another (Kshatriya) monk of a final (Pārājika) offense, either by himself or by inciting another, with the desire to cause him to fall from the Sasana, falls into a grave offense (Saᅅghādisesa).

Knowing that he has committed an offense, for as many days as he conceals it, for that many days he must undergo probation (parivāsa). Having completed the probation, he must practice penance (mānatta) for six nights in the Saᅅgha. After having practiced penance, a group of twenty monks must rehabilitate (abbhāna) that monk.

An offense is said to be concealed at dawn when it is endowed with ten factors: the occurrence of the offense, not being an expelled person, the absence of obstacles, the ability to confess, perceiving it as such, the desire to conceal, and the act of concealing.

## 3. Cĩvaraniddeso (Exposition of Robes)

Robes (cĩvara) are:
Linen cloth, silk cloth, cotton cloth, hemp cloth, coarse cloth, and wool cloth (blanket). These six types of cloth, along with those of a similar nature by birth, are allowable (for monks).

White linen cloth called dukšla, silk cloth from the Paᅡᅡuᅅᅡa region, silk cloth from the Somāra and Cĩna regions, cloth produced by psychic power, and cloth given by devas are suitable cloths corresponding to those six types such as linen and silk.

The three robes, the accessory cloth, the rain-cloth, the face towel, and the sitting cloth must be determined (adhiᅡᅡhāna); they should not be shared by ownership (vikappanā).

The bedding, the itch-covering cloth, and the three robes in this Sasana (should be determined). One should not remain separated from the three robes for even one day, nor from the sitting cloth for four months.

One should determine the saᅅghāᅡi by saying, "I determine this saᅅghāᅡi." If the robe is beyond reach (outside the hatthapāsa), one should say, "I determine that robe." This same method applies to the remaining robes.

A monk who wishes to determine a new robe, such as a saᅅghāᅡi, should first relinquish (paccuddharaᅅa) the old robe before determining the new one. The same applies to the determination of the alms-bowl.

One should say, "I relinquish that saᅅghāᅡi," or "I relinquish this saᅅghāᅡi." In this way, a wise person who knows the Vinaya should relinquish all robes by naming them.

The saᅅghāᅡi, at its minimum, must be five fist-spans (muᅡᅡhipafca) in length. At its maximum, a robe that is smaller than the Sugata's (the Buddha's) robe is also allowable.

In width, it should be three fist-spans; the measurement of the uttarāsaᅅga is the same. The antaravāsaka (inner robe) should also be five fist-spans in length; in width, two and a half cubits or two cubits is allowable.

The measurement of the sitting cloth (nisĩdana) should be two spans in length, one and a half spans in width, and one span for the border, according to the Sugata's span.

The measurement of the itch-covering cloth (kaᅅᅡupaᅡiccādi) should be two spans in width and four spans in length, according to the Sugata's span.

The measurement of the rain-cloth (vassikasāᅡika) is six spans in length and two and a half spans in width, according to the Sugata's span.

For these robes, a monk who makes them exceeding those measurements commits a Pācittiya offense involving cutting (chedana-pācittiya), where the excess must be cut off and the offense confessed. As for the bedding and face towels, they may be of any desired measurement.

There is no mention of the number or measurement for accessory cloths (parikkhāracola). Therefore, cloths suitable for sharing (vikappanā), such as bags, should be determined by calling them accessory cloths.

A saᅅghāᅡi made of new cloth or cloth equivalent to new should be double-layered. The uttarāsaᅅga and antaravāsaka should likewise be single-layered.

If made of old cloths taken out after a long time, the saᅅghāᅡi may be four-layered. The remaining two robes may be double-layered. In the case of rag-robes (paᅃsukšla), one may make as many layers as desired.

Among the three robes, if any two are sufficient to be cut (to the minimum size), those two should be cut. If only one is sufficient, that one should be cut. If all the robes are insufficient to be cut to the minimum size, one should take an additional layer (anvādhimādiyeyya). One should not determine and wear the three robes if they are neither cut nor provided with an additional layer.

In a village, in a house outside a village, in a storehouse for goods such as vehicles, in a long palace, in a gabled palace, in a boat, in a watchtower, in a pavilion, in an orchard, in a flower garden, among a group of merchants, in a field, in a threshing floor, at a tree, in the open air, or in a monastery—it is not proper to stay separated from the triple robes (ticīvara) without the formal consent of the monks (bhikkhu-sammuti).

The itch-cloth (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi) and the rainy-season cloth (vassikasāṭika) have a limit of the duration of the illness and the four months of the rainy season respectively. An upper covering, a requisite cloth, and a face towel may be used even if they have fringes or if they have a mark (kappabindu) that has not been properly dyed or pierced. A sitting cloth (nisīdana) may also be used even if it has a mark that has not been properly dyed or pierced.

The remaining five types of robes are only allowable if they have no fringes, are dyed, and have a mark (kappabindu) applied. A sitting cloth is only allowable if it has fringes.

All these procedures have been explained for a monk who carries the triple robes according to the Vinaya. One may also determine all robes by designating them as 'requisite cloths' (parikkhāracola).

Robbery, giving away, taking by trust (vissāsagāha), disrobing, revocation (paccuddhara), death, and the loss of the gender or the training—these are the causes for the loss of determination (adhiṭṭhāna) for all robes. For the triple robes (ticīvara), a hole as large as the fingernail of the little finger that passes through the fabric is also a cause for the loss of determination.

For a monk who wears garments made of kusa grass, bark, or wooden slats; a blanket made of human hair or animal hair; a garment made of owl wings; or a deer skin, there is an offense of grave transgression (thullaccaya).

A monk whose robes have been stolen is allowed to wear any kind of garment.

## 4. Description of Dyes (Rajananiddesa)

Regarding dyes:

The Blessed One has authorized six kinds of dyes: root dye, trunk dye, bark dye, leaf dye, fruit dye, and flower dye.

Among root dyes, all root dyes are allowable except for turmeric. Among trunk dyes, all trunk dyes are allowable except for those from the palmyra and the jackfruit vine. Among leaf dyes, all leaf dyes are allowable except for indigo leaves and henna leaves. Among bark dyes, all bark dyes are allowable except for Symplocos bark and Ventilago bark. Among flower dyes, all flower dyes are allowable except for safflower and Butea monosperma flowers.

## 5. Description of the Alms-bowl (Pattaniddesa)

Regarding the alms-bowl (patto ca):

There are two types of allowable alms-bowls by material: the iron bowl and the clay bowl. By size, there are three types: large (ukkaṭṭha), medium (majjhima), and small (omaka).

A large bowl holds alms-food cooked from two nāḷis of Magadhan rice, along with a proportional amount of curry and side dishes.

A medium bowl holds half as much as the large bowl. A small bowl holds half as much as the medium bowl. A bowl larger than the large size or smaller than the small size is not considered a bowl (for formal determination).

One may keep an extra bowl for a maximum of ten days. If that ten-day period is exceeded, it becomes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya).

The determination (adhiṭṭhāna) of a bowl is lost due to robbery, giving away, taking by trust (vissāsagāha), disrobing, death, revocation (paccuddhara), loss of gender, loss of training, or the presence of a hole.

One should not put away a bowl that is not dry, nor should one dry it in the sun (excessively). It should not be left in the hot sun, nor placed on the ground (without a stand), nor should it be hung up.

It is not proper to place the alms-bowl on the inner edge of the rim, the outer edge of the rim, on the lap, on an umbrella, on the feet, or on a bed or chair. One should not carry out rinse-water or discarded bones and meat in the alms-bowl. A person holding an alms-bowl in their hand should not push or open a door-leaf. Two alms-bowls may be placed one on top of the other on a floor-stand or on a well-prepared wooden bowl-stand. However, on the bare ground, a single alms-bowl may only be placed upside down. Alms-bowls made of wood, silver, gold, gems, or lapis lazuli; alms-bowls made of bronze, glaze (artificial stone), white tin, lead, crystal, or copper; alms-bowls made from human skulls; and alms-bowls made from pots or gourds—all these are improper and are said to be grounds for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

## 6. Explanation of Cups (Thālakaniddesa)
The explanation of cups is as follows: Three types of cups made of copper, iron, or clay are allowable. Cups made of wood, gold, silver, gems, or lapis lazuli are not allowable. Cups made of crystal, glaze (artificial stone), or bronze are allowable if they belong to laypeople or if they are the property of the Saṅgha (saṅghika). Gourd-cups and pot-cups are allowable for temporary use.

## 7. Explanation of Pavāraṇā

Pavāraṇā means:
While a monk is eating any of the five types of soft food, if he refuses [further food] in a certain posture, he is said to have "made a refusal" (pavārita). If he eats hard food or soft food that has not been made "leftover" (atiritta) according to Vinaya procedures (and is not the remains of a sick monk) in a posture other than that one, he commits a Pācittiya offense.

The five factors of Pavāraṇā are: eating, the food being one of the five types of soft food, it being offered, being within arm's reach (hatthapāsa), and refusing by either body or speech.

Cooked rice (odana), parched grain meal (sattu), sour gruel (kummāsa), fish (maccha), and meat (maṃsa) are called soft food (bhojana). Cooked rice and thick gruel made from the seven types of grain—sāli rice, vīhi rice, barley (yava), millet (kaṅgu), kudrūsa grain, varaka grain, and wheat (godhuma)—which can be eaten by hand, are also called odana (cooked rice).

Grains from grasses such as sāmāka are included under kudrūsa; maize is included under varaka; and wild rice (nīvāra) is included under sāli rice.

Meal made from roasted grains is called sattu. Sour gruel made from barley is called kummāsa. Only allowable meat is referred to as maṃsa. Any creature born in water is called maccha (fish).
144:
While eating any type of soft food, whether allowable or unallowable, a monk who refuses allowable soft food brought within arm's reach (hatthapāsa), either by naming the food or by saying "this [is enough]," is said to have "made a refusal" (pavārita).

Parched rice (lāja), snacks and rice made from that parched rice, the five kinds of cow products (gorasa), pure hard food (khajjaka) without meat, roasted rice, roasted flour, flattened rice (pothuka), rice made from bamboo seeds, etc.;
Rice made from grains other than the seven mentioned (such as bamboo seeds), gruel mixed with meat broth or fish broth, pure meat broth or fish broth, pure gruel, fruits, etc., do not cause Pavāraṇā.

A monk who has made a refusal (pavārita) should not, after rising from his seat, make food "leftover" (atiritta). A monk who has not yet eaten should also not make food "leftover." A monk who has previously made a certain hard or soft food "leftover" should not make that same food "leftover" again.

A Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) who makes allowable, received, lifted, and brought within arm's reach hard or soft food "leftover" should say: "Alametaṃ sabbaṃ—All this is enough for me."

One should not make food "leftover" while it is in the hands of a layperson or a novice (sāmaṇera). One may have another person make it "leftover." All monks, whether they have made a refusal or not, except for the Vinaya expert who performed the procedure, are permitted to eat that food which has been made "leftover."

## 9. Paṭiggāhaniddesa

Acceptance (paṭiggaha) must be endowed with these factors: the giver's intention to offer, being within the hatthapāsa (two and a half cubits), and the object being such that a man of medium strength can lift it. Only when the giver offers in three ways (by body, by an object connected to the body, or by throwing) and the receiver accepts in two ways (by body or by an object connected to the body) is it an acceptance endowed with the five factors.

Acceptance is not valid in the case of immovable objects, things growing in that very place (such as leaves not yet plucked from a tree), tiny leaves such as tamarind leaves, and loads too heavy to be carried.

Acceptance is nullified by giving up the training, death, change of sex, abandonment without concern, robbery, or giving to a layperson or a novice.
149:
A monk who consumes any kālika (food) that has not yet been formally accepted commits a pācittiya offense. However, pure water that is free from dust and not too thick may be drunk without being formally accepted. Furthermore, teeth tartar, eye wax, ear wax, salt (produced from the body), saliva, nasal mucus, phlegm, urine, and feces that are attached to the body and not yet detached may also be consumed without being formally accepted.

In times of emergency, such as a snake bite or poisoning, if there is no kappiyakāraka (attendant) to make things allowable, one may take feces, fine earth, urine, and ash by oneself and use them.

An offense of dukkaṭa is committed by bad habits such as shaking a fruit-bearing tree, holding a bowl containing unoffered food, going for alms with a bowl full of dust without it being accepted, picking up an item knowing it has not been accepted, storing unoffered items indoors, cooking by oneself, or cooking indoors with unoffered items.

## 10. Akappiyamaṃsaniddesa

Forbidden meats are: the meat of humans, elephants, horses, dogs, leopards, lions, tigers, hyenas, bears, and snakes—these ten types of meat are unallowable. Meat killed specifically for a member of the Order (uddissakata-maṃsa) and meat eaten without investigation or inquiry are also unallowable. Eating human meat entails a thullaccaya offense, while eating the remaining forbidden meats entails a dukkaṭa offense.
150:
The bones, blood, skin, and hair of those animals whose meat is unallowable are also not allowable. Only the offense incurred by eating meat specifically dedicated to oneself (uddissakata-maṃsa) is an offense with intention (sacittaka). The offenses incurred by eating other types of meat are offenses without intention (acittaka), occurring even if there is no specific intent. 

## 11. Explanation of Forfeiture (Nissaggiyaniddesa)
Regarding forfeiture (nissaggiya): If one exchanges a non-monetary object for money (rūpiya), or money for another non-monetary object, or money for money, in this Dispensation, an offense of forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya) is incurred because of that money. Gold, silver, coins (kahāpaṇa), and various types of currency used in trade are called 'rūpiya'. Allowable objects such as cloth and pearls, as well as other objects that are grounds for an offense of wrong-doing, are called 'non-monetary' (arūpiya). 

If one enters into buying, selling, or exchanging by saying, "Take this rice, etc., and give this cloth, etc.," or "Do this work," or "Bring this item," or "Eat this meal, etc., and act in this way," or "I give this item, give that item in return," an offense of forfeiture and confession is incurred. 

If one diverts a gain already intended for the Saṅgha to oneself, an offense of forfeiture and confession is incurred. If one diverts it to another individual, a confession (pācittiya) offense is incurred. If one diverts it to another Saṅgha or to a shrine (cetiya), an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred. If one uses a forfeiture-object without first forfeiting it, an offense of wrong-doing is incurred. If one does not return a forfeited item, perceiving it as one's own property, an offense of wrong-doing is incurred. If one does not return it with the intention to steal, other offenses such as defeat (pārājika), grave offense (thullaccaya), or wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are incurred.

## 12. Pācittiyaniddesa

Pācittiya offenses are: lying, abusive speech, and likewise conveying slander; reciting the Dhamma word-by-word (with an unordained person); sleeping under the same roof; complaining and disparaging.

Striking with the palm, disrespect, causing remorse, entering a village without permission, and eating out of turn in regards to meals.

Going away without putting away the monastery's bedding, traveling on a journey with a woman, and sitting alone with a woman.

Frightening, hitting, speaking evasively when questioned, harassing, revealing a grave offense (duṭṭhullāpatti), concealing it, playing in water, expelling from a monastery, and sleeping near a monk who should not be disturbed—these are declared as pācittiya offenses.

## 13. Samaṇakappaniddesa

Samaṇakappa means: destroying a group of living plants (bhūtagāma) entails a pācittiya offense. Seeds (bījagāma) made allowable by means of nails, fire, or knives are allowable ascetic practices (samaṇakappiya) for monks.

That bhūtagāma arises from five types: root-germs, trunk-germs, seed-germs, bud-germs, and joint-germs. Destroying the five types of seeds that have been separated from the plant entails a dukkaṭa offense.
152:
A fruit whose seed has been removed, or a fruit whose seed is too immature to grow, is allowable even if the kappiya procedure has not been performed. For fruits with seeds attached to shells or rinds, the kappiya procedure should be performed on the outer shell.

Among seeds that are connected together in a pot or in the ground, if the kappiya procedure is performed on one seed, it is considered performed on all of them.

If roots and leaves grow from ginger or similar items that were placed in sand after the kappiya procedure was performed, the kappiya procedure must be performed again because that ginger has become bhūtagāma once more.

Moss or algae arising in water, whether with leaves or without leaves, and moss with two or three leaves arising on cetiyas and such, are simply bhūtagāma. Even if it is a primary seed, once roots and leaves have emerged, it is simply bhūtagāma.

Moss on the outside of water pots and such, and unbloomed mushrooms, are bases for the dukkaṭa offense. A bloomed mushroom, however, does not deserve to be called a dukkaṭa.

A pācittiya offense is committed by a monk who destroys and takes lac, resin, or mushrooms from a living tree, or by a monk who cuts (carves) letters into that living tree.
153:
133. It is not allowable to squeeze coconut trees and the like with wooden monkey-paw tools and the like, nor is it allowable to cut (destroy) or tie knots in grass and the like.

134. One should not speak by specifying a particular thing, saying to a person regarding plants (bhūtagāma) or seeds (bījagāma): "Cut [this], destroy [this], pluck [this]," or "Split [this], pierce [this], cook [this]."

135. It is allowable to speak in this way: "Make this allowable (kappiya)," "Take this," "Bring this," "Give this," or "Clean this."

## 14. Bhūminiddesa (Description of Grounds)

Regarding grounds (bhūmi):
136. There are four types of allowable grounds (kuṭi): Sammuti, Ussāvanantikā, Gonisādikā, and Gahapati. In these allowable grounds, both stored food and food cooked by laypeople are allowable.

137. One should arrange to obtain an allowable Kappiya-kuṭi in a monastery—whether it belongs to the Saṅgha or to an individual—where an offense of sleeping together (sahaseyya) might occur.

138. While a monastery of the Saṅgha or of an individual is being constructed, one should lay the first brick or the first pillar while saying: "We are making a Kappiya-kuṭi, we are making a Kappiya-kuṭi." Such a construction is called Ussāvanantikā (a hut completed at the end of the proclamation).
154:
139. Generally, a monastery (ārāma) that is unfenced or entirely without an enclosure is called 'Gonisādī' because it is a place where cattle can enter and stay. A hut designated by the Saṅgha is called a 'Sammuti-kuṭi'.

140. A house or building given by others (excluding monks) or belonging to them, intended for the purpose of an allowable hut, is to be known as a 'Gahapati-kuṭi'.

141. The two types of food, namely 'timed food' (yāvakālika) and 'evening food' (yāmakālika), which were previously obtained and then mixed with 'seven-day food' (sattāhakālika) such as ghee or 'lifetime food' (yāvajīvika) stored in a non-allowable hut, reach the state of being 'stored-within' (antovuttha).

142. If a monk cooks such 'lifetime food' together with those 'stored-within' items like ghee, it is allowable for seven days if it does not contain solid food (āmisa) like rice. However, if it is mixed with solid food, it reaches the state of being 'self-cooked' (sāma-pākata).

143. An Ussāvanantikā hut established by pillars and the like remains valid even if those original pillars are removed, as long as it stands on other pillars or bricks.

144. If all pillars or bricks are removed, the Ussāvanantikā hut becomes a 'discarded site' (losing its status as an allowable ground). A Gonisādī hut becomes a discarded site if it is fenced, and the remaining two types of huts become discarded sites if their roofs are destroyed.

## 15. Upajjhāyācariyavatta-niddesa (Description of Duties to the Preceptor and Teacher)

Regarding the duties to the Preceptor and Teacher:

145. A virtuous monk living in dependence on a Preceptor (upajjhāya) and a Teacher (ācariya) should always provide tooth-wood, a seat, water for washing the face, and congee (yāgu) in the early morning.

146. He should perform the appropriate duties regarding the alms-bowl, when entering, walking in, or returning from the village, and regarding the seat, foot-stool, foot-scrubbing shard, sandals, and robes.

147. He should likewise perform duties regarding water for use and drinking, the places for defecation and urination, cleaning the monastery, and again in preparing the sleeping places and seats.

148. A monk cleaning the monastery must not shake out bedding in an upwind direction, in places where many people gather, or near drinking water.

149. He should perform duties at the time of bathing, duties to be done for the teacher who has finished bathing, and during the boiling of dye, washing of robes, and sewing of robes. A monk dyeing a robe should not depart while dye-drops still remain on the robe.
156:
One should not give an alms-bowl, robes, or any other requisite (parikkhāra) to a person (disliked by the teacher) without asking the teacher, nor should one receive such items from them.

One should not make such a person one's follower, nor follow behind that person. One should not carry alms-food for that person, nor have that person carry alms-food for oneself.

It is not allowable to perform or have performed any task, large or small, for oneself or for others, such as massage (parikamma) or hair-cutting, without asking the teacher.

It is not allowable for a monk who wishes to go to a village, a cemetery, outside the boundary (nissīma), or to another region, or for a monk who wishes to perform his own tasks, to go or act without asking the teacher.

One should dispel any dissatisfaction (arati), wrong view (diṭṭhi), or remorse (kukkucca) that arises in the teacher. One should also take care of the Saṅgha's business and duties.

One should attend to teachers who are ill and should wait upon them until they recover from their illness. If one neglects these duties out of disrespect in any of these matters, it is said that one incurs a Dukkaṭa offense.

## 16. Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānika-niddesa (Description of Duties regarding the Toilet and Urinal)

Vaccapassāvaṭṭhānika refers to the conduct in the toilet (vaccakuṭi) and urinal (passāvakuṭi).

In defecating, one should not follow the order of seniority (it is not necessary). In the toilet, urinal, and bathing places, one is entitled to use them according to the order of arrival.
157:
One should not enter the toilet with the under-robe lifted, nor should one enter hastily. One should enter only after coughing. One should lift the under-robe only after standing firmly on the foot-rests.

One should not defecate while groaning (making 'inn-inn' sounds). One should not defecate while chewing tooth-wood. One should not discharge both feces and urine outside the respective vessels.

One should not drop the scraper (kanu-taṃ) into the cesspit. One should not spit into the urinal. One should not scrape with a rough scraper, and one should wash away any smeared feces.

One should not exit hastily. One should not exit with the under-robe lifted. One should not wash oneself making a 'capu-capu' sound. One should also clear away any litter.

## 17. Āpucchakaraṇa-niddesa (Description of Asking Permission)

Regarding Āpucchakaraṇa:

Without being invited by an Elder (thera), one should not recite the Pātimokkha. One should not preach the Dhamma. One should not ask or answer questions.

If a senior monk arrives while one is preaching after having already asked permission, there is no need to ask for permission again. Similarly, there is no need to ask again when performing the Anumodanā (thanksgiving) at a meal place.

A monk living with an Elder in the same monastery should not recite texts, nor give instructions in the Pali Canon or ask about the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) without asking permission.
158:
(Without asking a senior monk), one should not preach the Dhamma, light a lamp, or extinguish a lamp; nor should one open or close a window or a door.

A monk walking on the walking path (caṅkama) with a senior should also turn back facing the senior. That junior monk should not let the corner of his double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) touch the senior.

## 18. Exposition on Nakedness (Nagganiddesa)
Regarding nakedness:
One should not walk on the road, eat, drink, chew, or lick while naked. One should not receive or give (offerings), nor should one pay homage or allow others to pay homage (to oneself) while naked.

One should not have others perform preparatory tasks (parikamma) such as scrubbing the body while naked, nor should one do it oneself. Among the three types of coverings, performing preparatory tasks is permissible in water-coverings and steam-room (jantāghara) coverings. Covering with cloth is permissible for all activities, such as walking on the road.

## 19. Exposition on the Method of Bathing (Nhānakappaniddesa)
Regarding the method of bathing:
One should not bathe directly in front of seniors, nor upstream (or upwind) from them. A junior monk coming out of the water should give way to seniors entering the water.

A monk bathing should not rub his body against walls, pillars, trees, or (scrubbing) boards. He should not rub his body with a wooden "monkey-hand" (gandhabba-hattha) or a string of kuruvindaka powder beads.
159:
One should not rub with a scrubber that has teeth like a crocodile's (makaradantaka), nor with another person's body.
Pieces of broken pottery, broken bricks, and rolls of cloth are permissible.
Scrubbing with the palm of the hand is permissible for all monks, whether healthy or ill.
For an ill monk, a scrubber without teeth is permissible.
For rubbing the feet, stones, sea foam (pumice), and pottery shards are permissible.

## 20. Exposition on Those Not to be Saluted (Avandiyaniddesa)
Regarding those not to be saluted:
A suspended person (ukkhittaka), an unordained person (anupasampanna) such as a layman or a novice, a senior of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsa), a woman, a junior monk, a monk undergoing penance (parivāsa, etc.) for a grave offense (garuka-āpatti), and a eunuch (paṇḍaka) are those who should not be saluted.

## 21. Exposition on Skins (Cammaniddesa)
Regarding skins:
The skins of deer, goats, and sheep are permissible for use. The rohita-deer, eṇī-deer, spotted deer, and barking deer are also included in the deer category.

If skins other than the three permitted types are used (on beds or chairs), it constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For bags and sandals, all skins except human skin are permissible.

## 22. Exposition on Sandals (Upāhananiddesa)
Regarding sandals:
In the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), new sandals sewn in layers are not permissible.
Within the monastery grounds (ārāma), wearing sandals is permissible for all monks.
For an ill monk, wearing sandals is permissible in all places.

Sandals that are entirely blue (or dark), white, yellow, red, or black; sandals dyed repeatedly with many dyes or with dyes of many names;

Sandals that are entirely crimson, ornate sandals, sandals decorated with blue, yellow, etc., on the edges; sandals with the color of a partridge's wing, sandals with curved tips like sheep or goat horns (are not permissible).
160:
Sandals that are entirely blue, entirely white, entirely yellow, entirely red, or entirely black; sandals dyed repeatedly with many dyes or with dyes of many names (should not be worn).

Sandals that are entirely crimson (mañjeṭṭhika), ornate with floral or vine patterns, sandals with straps of blue, yellow, etc.; sandals with a mottled color like a partridge's wing, sandals with straps like sheep or goat horns (should not be worn).

Sandals with heel-covers, sandals with straps tied up to the calf (boots), sandals stuffed with cotton, sandals with covers wrapped only over the soles, sandals sewn all around with peacock feathers (should not be worn).

Sandals with straps like a scorpion's tail, sandals covered all around with the skins of lions, tigers, otters, deer, or leopards; sandals covered with the skins of cats, squirrels, or owls; and movable wooden sandals—if any monk wears or carries these, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

One may use sandals after wiping away the blue or other colors, either entirely or partially, or after removing the heel-covers and such.

## 23. Exposition on Not Looking (Anolokiyaniddesa)
Regarding not looking:
One should not look at a woman's private parts or the face of a woman offering alms-food with a mind full of lust. If one looks at another's bowl with the intent to disparage, or looks at one's own face in a mirror or a bowl of water, that monk commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
161:
## 24. Exposition on Collyrium Containers (Añjanīniddesa)
Regarding collyrium containers:
182. A collyrium container (añjanī) that is round, eight-sided, or sixteen-sided is permissible. A smooth collyrium container without floral or vine patterns is permissible. Three lines (grooves) at the base of the container and a single line at the neck for tying the closure are permissible.

183. In this collyrium container, any figures such as women, men, four-footed animals, or birds; floral patterns; crocodile-tooth (saw-tooth) shapes; cow-urine-track shapes, half-moon shapes, or other such elaborate designs are not permissible.

184. It is permissible to sew a collyrium bag, as well as a razor bag or a key bag, with thread of a single color. A collyrium probe (salākā) without ornate figures or floral patterns is also permissible.

185. Collyrium containers made of conch-shell, horn, bone (except human bone), reed, or ivory are permissible; likewise, those made of fruit, wood, bamboo, lac, copper, or iron are permissible. Collyrium probes, smoking pipes, small knife handles, and nose-medicine tubes made of these materials like conch-shell, etc., are also permissible.

## 25. Exposition on Unallowable Beds and Seats (Akappiyasayananiddesa)
Regarding unallowable beds and seats:
187. A long-legged chair (āsandī), a mattress stuffed with the three types of cotton (tūlī), a throne (pallaṅka) with legs shaped like lions, tigers, etc., a plain white wool cover without patterns (paṭika), a large black wool carpet with long fleece (gonaka), a wool cover ornate with patterns (cittaka), a wool cover embroidered with flowers (paṭalī), a wool cover ornate with animal figures (vikatī), a wool cover with fleece on both sides (uddalomi), a wool cover with fleece on one side (ekantalomikā).

188. A wool carpet large enough for sixteen dancers (kutta), a silk cover embroidered with gold and silver threads (koseyya), a cover woven with gold thread inside silk (kaṭṭissa), covers spread on elephants, horses, or chariots, a rug made of black antelope skins sewn together (ajinappaveṇī), and a noble cover made of the skin of the kadalī-deer (kadalī-miga-pavara-atthara).

189. A cover with a red canopy above and red pillows at both ends (head and foot)—a monk who uses these unallowable beds and seats commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
162:
A covering with a red canopy above and red pillows at both the head and foot—these floor coverings are not suitable for monks. For a monk who uses them, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

With the exception of the three types of coverings—the long chair (āsandī), the mattress (tūlī), and the couch (pallaṅka)—it is permissible to sit on coverings belonging to laypeople in places where the Dhamma is preached, in the refectory, and in houses within the village. If it is a covering spread on the ground, it is also permissible to sleep on it.

Square chairs with seven parts (four legs, two sides, and a backrest), chairs with five parts, and chairs with high legs are permissible. It is permissible to sit on couches and chairs stuffed with cotton only within a house in the village.

The five types of bolsters (bhisi) stuffed with cloth, bark-fiber, hair, leaves, or grass, and encased in a robe-cloth bag, are permissible in all places.

The use of three types of cotton, the five types of bolster-stuffing, and the feathers of animals or birds is permitted for pillows (bimbohana). However, for a leather cushion (masuraka), the other stuffings are permitted with the exception of the three types of cotton.

In hair-stuffing, one should not mix human hair; in leaf-stuffing, one should not use only flowers or only tamāla leaves. One should also not sit on a puffed-up seat without careful investigation.

## 26. Samānāsanikaniddesa (Explanation of Sitting Together)

Regarding sitting together (samānāsanika):

The sitting together on a single couch or chair is permitted for two monks who are within three years of seniority of each other (i.e., two years older or two years younger). Therefore, a monk of five years' seniority is allowed to sit together with a senior monk of seven years or a junior monk of three years.
163:
The Blessed One allowed sitting on a long seat with all others, excluding eunuchs (paṇḍaka), women, and hermaphrodites (ubhatovyañjanaka). A seat that is sufficient for three monks to sit on is called the minimum 'long seat' (dīghāsana). Two monks are permitted to sit together on a couch or a chair.

## 27. Asaṃvāsikaniddesa (Explanation of Non-communion)

Regarding non-communion (asaṃvāsika):

It has been explained that the following are those with whom there is no communion (asaṃvāsika): a suspended (ukkittaka) monk, an unordained person (anupasampanna), a bhikkhunī, one who has committed a parājika offense (chinnamūlaka), one of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), one standing outside the boundary (sīmā), one standing in the air, and the eleven types of persons who are excluded from ordination (abhabba).

## 28. Kammaniddesa (Explanation of Legal Acts)

Regarding legal acts (kamma):

There are four types: an unlawful act by an incomplete assembly, an unlawful act by a complete assembly, a lawful act by an incomplete assembly, and a lawful act by a complete assembly. Only the fourth, the lawful act by a complete assembly (samagga-dhammakamma), is permitted; for the remaining acts, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

Five types of Sangha have been clearly defined: a group of four, a group of five, a group of ten, a group of twenty, and a group of more than twenty.

Among these five types of Sangha, a group of four is competent to perform all acts except for rehabilitation (abbhāna), ordination (upasampadā), and the invitation (pavarāṇā). A group of five is competent to perform all acts except for rehabilitation (abbhāna) and ordination (upasampadā) in the central regions (majjhimadesa).
164:
A group of ten is competent to perform all legal acts except for rehabilitation (abbhāna). The others (the group of twenty and the group of more than twenty) have been explained as being competent for all legal acts.

In a legal act that must be performed by four monks, four regular (pakaṭatta) monks are required for the act to be valid. Other monks within that boundary are eligible to give their consent (chanda). This same principle applies to acts that must be performed by a group of five and so on.

In performing acts such as probation (parivāsa), which must be performed by a group of four or more, if the quorum is completed by including a monk with whom there is no communion, a monk who is the subject of the act, or a monk who has committed a grave offense (garuka-āpatti), then that act is invalid and there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

One should protest an unlawful act (if there is no danger). If there is danger, two or three monks should clearly manifest their own (disapproving) view. If there is only one monk, he should make a mental determination. If there are more than three monks, they must certainly protest the unlawful act.

A protest made in the midst of the Sangha by a monk who is the subject of the act, a monk with whom there is no communion, a monk who is mentally deranged, or a monk who is oppressed by painful feelings, is not valid.

If a regular (pakaṭatta) monk, staying within the same boundary and belonging to the same communion, informs even the monk nearest to him (of his disapproval), the protest is valid.

If one protests in the presence of the Sangha for the purpose of ruining a lawful act, or if one stays away from the assembly without giving one's physical presence or consent (chanda), there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

## 29. Explanation of Avoiding Wrong Livelihood (Micchājīvavivajjananiddesa)
(209) A monk should not give wood, bamboo, fruit, flowers, bathing powder, face-washing water, clay, tooth-sticks, and so on, as a means of currying favor with families. (210) One should not make a living by fondling or coaxing children; by being a person of false speech with little truth, like a bean soup; by the art of reading the signs of house sites or grounds; by acting as a messenger on long journeys at the behest of others; or by acting as a servant on short journeys. (211) One should not make a living by giving gifts in expectation of gain, by giving food in return for food, by practicing medicine, or by any other arts censured by the Fully Enlightened One. (212) One should avoid requisites that arise through begging, seeking in improper ways, boasting of non-existent superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), pretending to be wonderful to inspire awe, or through corrupting families.

## 30. Explanation of Duties (Vattaniddesa)
Regarding duties: (213) A visiting monk (āgantuka) should not enter the monastery grounds wearing sandals, carrying an umbrella, with his head covered, or with his robe placed on his head. (214) He should not wash his feet with drinking water. He should pay respect to the resident monks (āvāsika) who are his seniors. He should ask for the lodgings assigned to him. (215) A monk who is about to depart should put away wooden and clay items, close the dwelling, and depart after informing others about the lodgings. (216) If there is no one to inform, he should depart only after making the place well-secured. To depart otherwise is improper.
166:
A monk who is about to travel must put away wooden and earthenware articles, close the monastery, and ask permission regarding the lodgings. If there is no one to ask permission from, he should store them well and securely before departing. To depart otherwise is not proper for that monk.

A resident monk should prepare a seat for a senior visiting monk. He should place water for washing the feet and so forth, as well as the bowl and robes, nearby. He should go out to welcome him, receive the bowl and robes, and offer drinking water. He should pay respects to the visiting monk and prepare the lodgings.

He should inform the visitor whether the monastery has been inhabited before or not, about the alms-resort village and non-resort areas, the places for defecation and urination, the established agreements, and the families designated as 'Sekha' (learners).

He should also inform him about the time for entering and leaving the monastery, and about the water for use and drinking. If the visitor is junior to him, he may point out all these things while remaining seated.

## 31. Explanation of Vikappanā (Formal Assignment)
Regarding the performance of Vikappanā—

It is taught that there are two types of Vikappanā: in the presence (of the recipient) and in the absence (of the recipient). A monk wishing to perform Vikappanā in the presence should say to a competent monk: "I assign this robe to you (imaṃ cīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ vikappemi)."
167:
By merely performing Vikappanā to this extent, it is only proper for the purpose of storage; it is not yet proper for use and so forth. This is because that competent monk has not yet performed the withdrawal (paccuddhāra).

Only after that competent monk has performed the withdrawal by saying, "Use my property, or give it away, or do as you see fit," is it proper for use and so forth.

There is another type of Vikappanā in the presence:
In the presence of one monk,
Taking the name of one
Among the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika).

One should say: "I assign this robe to the monk Tissa (or to the nun Tissā, the novice Tissa, the female novice Tissā, or the female trainee Tissā)."

That competent monk should then say: "Use the property of the monk Tissa (or the nun Tissā, the novice Tissa, the female novice Tissā, or the female trainee Tissā), or give it away, or do as you see fit."

When performing Vikappanā in the absence, one should say in the presence of a monk:
"I give this robe to you for the purpose of Vikappanā."
168:
That competent monk (the Vinaya-expert) should ask: "Who is your firm friend or your acquaintance?" The other monk (the owner of the robe) should reply: "It is the monk Tissa," or "the nun Tissā," or "the novice Tissa," or "the female novice Tissā," or "the female trainee Tissā."

Then that competent monk, having assigned it by saying, "I give it to Tissa (the monk or trainee, etc.)," must perform the withdrawal (paccuddhāra) by saying, "Use the property of the monk Tissa (or the nun, etc.), or give it away, or do as you see fit."

Knowing the distinction between far and near, and between singular and plural,
One should apply the terms "etaṃ, imaṃ" (this) or "etāni, imāni" (these) accordingly in this Vikappanā.

For ten days, or one month, or five months after the Kaṭhina has been spread,
If a person who is short of robes has the expectation of obtaining robes, for a full month,
A robe that has not been formally determined (adhiṭṭhita) or assigned (vikappita) does not cause an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya).

## 32. Explanation of Nissaya (Dependence)
Regarding Nissaya—

A competent monk with five years of seniority has no duty to be performed under dependence.
An incompetent monk, even for his whole life, must live only in dependence (on a teacher).
169:
Placing the robe over one shoulder, paying homage with joined palms, and sitting in a squatting position, one should say three times: "Venerable sir, be my teacher. I shall live in dependence on the venerable one."

Dependence is terminated due to (the pupil or teacher) departing for another place, joining another sect, disrobing, passing away, being expelled by the teacher, or reuniting with one's preceptor (upajjhāya).

One should not live in dependence on a shameless person (alajji). A monk arriving at a new place should wait for four or five days to ascertain if the monks there are of a similar virtuous nature (lajji).

A monk traveling a long distance, a sick monk, a monk attending to the sick who has been requested to do so, and a monk who finds comfort while dwelling in a forest monastery—if they do not find a teacher of similar nature, they are permitted to live without taking dependence until they meet such a teacher (or until the full moon of the rainy season).

## 33. Explanation of Kāyabandhana (Waistband)
Regarding the waistband—

If one enters a village without a waistband, one commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one enters due to a lapse in mindfulness, one must fasten the waistband at the very place where one remembers.
170:
There are two types of waistbands: the paṭṭikā (flat band) and the sūkarantaka (braided/cylindrical like a pig's tail). A flat strip of cloth is suitable as a paṭṭikā, and a single cord is suitable as a sūkarantaka.

Waistbands with designs like fish-bones or date-palm leaves, and plain smooth waistbands, are permitted. Fringes may be kept up to four, and a double-threaded cord at both ends may also be used.

A waistband woven with double threads showing patterns such as flowers or crab-eyes is not proper.

At the opening of the fringes, extraordinary shapes such as a water-pot shape or a makara-mouth shape are not proper. At the two ends of the waistband-buckle (vidha), except for the water-pot shape for durability and simple lines, other ornate figures are not proper.

Waistbands shaped like a water-snake's head, a muraja-drum, or a lute-neck, and those with many cords, are not proper. However, for the fringes, only the drum and lute-neck shapes are proper.

Waistband-buckles (vidha) made of bamboo, ivory, horn, bone, wood, lac, fruit, mother-of-pearl, thread, reed, or bronze are proper. Robe-buttons (ganṭhika) made of the same materials like bamboo and so forth are also proper.

## 34. Explanation of Earth (Pathavī-niddesa)

Regarding the explanation of earth—

Earth is of two kinds: natural earth (jāta) and unnatural earth (ajāta). Pure fine clay or dust that has not been burnt, earth with a high proportion of fine clay or dust, and heaps of dust or fine clay that have been wet by rain for more than four months are called natural earth (jāta-pathavī).

Pure gravel, stones, pebbles, potsherds, sand, burnt earth, earth mostly consisting of gravel etc., and heaps of fine clay or dust wet by rain for less than four months are called the second kind, unnatural earth (ajāta-pathavī).

If two-thirds of a soil is fine clay, it is called earth with much fine clay. The same method should be understood for earth with much dust, etc.

A monk who perceives natural earth as natural earth and digs it commits a Pācittiya offense. For one who is in doubt or perceives it as unnatural earth (but digs natural earth), there is a Dukkaṭa offense. The same applies to commanding others to dig.

For a monk digging himself, an offense is committed with every stroke (every time the tool hits). If he commands once, only one offense is committed; if he commands many times, an offense is committed with every word spoken.

It is not a fault to command by specifying a place, saying "Dig this place," "Dig this root," "Dig (a pond) here," or "Pull out the stump."
172: It is not allowable to command by specifying a place saying, "Dig this place, dig this root, dig a pond here, or light a fire here." It is allowable to say such words as, "Know the hole for this post," "Bring the fine clay," or "Make it allowable (kappiya)." It is allowable to destroy a thin layer of dry mud etc. that is not connected to the ground below. It is also allowable to destroy thin liquid mud that can be scooped up and poured with a pot. One should not destroy earthworm casts, termite-mound clay, mouse-hole dirt, or clods of earth that have been wet by rain for more than four months. The same applies to collapsed banks near water in ponds etc., dust clinging to stone slabs, dust fallen in new rock pools, termite mounds, and clay walls in the open (if wet for more than four months, they should not be destroyed). A brick wall is generally treated as earth with potsherds. It is not allowable to shake the earth violently to pull out posts etc., to destroy earth with a stream of urine, or to level uneven ground. It is not allowable to scrub with brooms, to drive in thorns etc., to destroy earth saying "I will show you," or to step heavily to leave footprints on a walkway (caṅkama).
173:
It is not allowable for a monk with a skin disease to rub his limbs against a broken bank etc., nor is it allowable to rub the earth to wash his hands.

Pulling out posts straight up, rolling stones etc., dragging branches etc., cutting or splitting wood and creepers are allowable for a monk with a pure mind (without the intention to destroy the earth). Pouring urine etc., and placing a wet hand on the ground to pick up dust are also allowable.

It is allowable to put fire in a potsherd or a brick bowl that is not fuel. When unable to hold the fire, it is allowable to let it fall onto the ground.

## 35. Explanation of Requisites (Parikkhāra-niddesa)

Regarding requisites—

It is not allowable to sew an umbrella on both inside and outside with threads of five colors, nor to cut designs like sea-monsters (makara) or half-moons on the umbrella cloth.

It is not allowable to make designs like a water-pot or a wild animal, or any inscriptions on the handle. However, making a bud-like shape like a mushroom on the base of the handle is allowable.

It is allowable to sew an umbrella with thread of a single color, or to bind the umbrella frame for firmness. Making an inscription (ring) on the handle for binding (a cord) is also allowable.

It is not allowable to have designs like ears of grain, chain links, or other special needlework on the borders or the seams of a robe. In making the allowable mark (kappabindu), special treatments like making them in a row or in a flower-like cluster are also not allowable.
174:
The patches for the button (gaṇṭhi) and the loop (pāsaka) should only be square. It is not allowable to sew them in the shape of a stupa, a mallet, a crab's eye, or other special designs.

Threads protruding from the corners of the button and loop patches and the knots made from them are allowable only if they are not prominent. One should not add perfume, oil, or lac to the robe dye.

A dyed robe should not be rubbed with a conch shell, a masāragalla stone, or any other object. It should not be rubbed while in the dyeing trough, nor beaten with a fist.

After dyeing the robe, the threads attached to the borders and corners should be cut off. Except for one line on the umbrella-shaped lid of a water-filter (dhammakaraṇa), other lines or designs are not allowable.

Large or small beads are not allowable on a crochet hook or a small knife. However, a dividing line on the knife handle is allowable.

Floral designs etc. on the fire-drill and its base are not allowable, nor is making the circumference of a bowl-stand ornate like a wall. On a walking stick, except for two lines at the bottom and a mushroom-like shape at the top, no decorative work like mountain peaks etc. is allowable on walking sticks or needle-cases.

No decorative work like floral designs etc. is forbidden on pillows, bolsters, couches, benches, and other bedding or seating; nor on brooms, waste baskets, dye-pots, drinking water pots, foot-washing benches, foot-scrubbing potsherds, bowl-stands, bowl-covers, palmyra fans, or square fans.

In a monastery, even gold-work is permitted on parts like door-leaves; what need is there to mention other forms of beautification?
175:
It is not prohibited to use oil containers such as those made of ivory, tubes, or gourds, which are devoid of male or female figures and have a smooth appearance with floral patterns or similar designs.

## 36. Bhesajjaniddesa (Exposition on Medicine)

The meaning of the term 'Bhesajja' is as follows:

It is not proper to perform medical treatment, give medicine, or provide medical prescriptions to the general public. However, it is proper to provide medical treatment using medicine obtained through alms-round, medicine obtained by request, or one's own medicine for fellow Dhamma-practitioners (sahadhammika), parents, the attendants of those parents, those who live depending on a monk, and monastery attendants (veyyāvaccakara).

For relatives of the seven ancestral lines, such as paternal uncles (elder or younger), maternal aunts (elder or younger), elder brothers, younger brothers, elder sisters, and younger sisters, if they have their own medicine, they should be treated with that medicine. If they do not have medicine, one's own medicine should be given to them temporarily (with the understanding that it should be returned).

This is because actions such as corrupting families, making requests, or providing medical treatment do not constitute an offense when they concern relatives related to one's own parents.

It is not prohibited to give alms-food that has not yet been partaken of (anāmaṭṭha) to the six types of persons starting with parents, as well as to rebels, dacoits, and rulers.

When performing Paritta (protection) for those who are not relatives, it should be done using only their own thread and water; it should not be done with one's own thread and water. If requested to recite Paritta, one should recite the Parittas contained within the Dispensation, such as the Ratana Sutta.

If someone is sent to request, "Please come and administer the precepts, preach the Dhamma, or recite Paritta," it is proper to go and perform the administration of precepts, the preaching of Dhamma, and the recitation of Paritta.
176:
## 37. Uggahaniddesa (Exposition on Taking)

Regarding 'Uggaha' (Taking/Accepting):
For a monk who accepts the ten kinds of precious gems (ratana) for the sake of new construction (navakamma), a stupa (cetiya), the Saṅgha, other individuals, or a group (gaṇa), there is an offense of Dukkaṭa (wrongdoing).

Among those precious gems, if gold and silver are accepted for one's own sake, there is an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya (forfeiture and confession). If the remaining eight kinds of gems are accepted (for one's own sake), there is an offense of Dukkaṭa. If an offering is made with the words, "I give this for the stupa" or "I give this for the new construction," without mentioning the group, the Saṅgha, or individuals by name, it should not be rejected. One should inform the kappiyakārakas (attendants), saying, "These donors speak in this manner."

When fields, lands, ponds, or slaves, cattle, and so on are offered, one should reject them (as unallowable) and accept them only through the proper sequence of allowable speech (kappiya-vohāra). If it is stated, "I give these fields and so on to the monastery," it is allowable.

Constructing new canals, fields, or ponds, or removing silt from an old pond, building embankments, and reinforcing them (if intended for the four requisites) is unallowable.

Taking an excessive portion from an old field, or initiating the demand for money by saying, "Give this much money," regarding crops from a new field whose portions have not yet been defined, is unallowable for both oneself and others.

Without saying words such as "plow" or "sow," defining the land by saying, "For this much land, this much portion (of the harvest) should be given," is also unallowable (for that monk).
177:
If, while the crops grown on a portion of land are being offered with the words 'Please take this much amount,' a monk measures the extent of the field with rods and ropes, or stands near the threshing floor to guard it, or causes the grain to be transported, or stores it in granaries and such, then that grain becomes unallowable only for the monk who managed it in such a way.

If a monk stores any property belonging to laypeople, or even property belonging to his parents, in the capacity of a storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), he commits an offense of Pācittiya. However, allowable items such as clothing belonging to parents must certainly be stored; one has the right to store them by treating them as one's own property. Even if requested, 'Please store this,' one must refuse. If they drop it and leave, one has the right to guard it, considering it as one's 'responsibility' (palibodha).

If one's own carpenters and others working in the monastery, or those who are favorites of the king, out of affection request, 'Please store our requisites or bedding,' one should not perform the storage out of affection or fear; it is only proper to show them a secure place. If they drop the items by force and leave, they should be stored. If precious gems or items regarded as gems are lost within such a monastery or rest-house, people tend to suspect the monk. If such items are found on the road or in the forest, one should act appropriately, knowing that the owner will come (it is said).
178:
Inside a monastery or one's own dwelling, if one finds a precious gem (ratana) or an item regarded as a gem, one should take and store it. The same applies if such a gem is found on the road or in the forest. If it is known that the owners are not coming to retrieve it, one should perform what is appropriate.

## 38. Kuladūsananiddesa (Exposition on Corrupting Families)

Regarding 'Dūsana' (Corruption):
For a monk who gives flowers, bamboo, fruits, powder, tooth-sticks, or clay for the sake of currying favor with laypeople (saṅgaha), there is an offense of Kuladūsana Dukkaṭa.

Among these items such as flowers, if a monk gives heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa) belonging to the Saṅgha as if he were the owner, he commits an offense of Thullaccaya (grave offense). If he gives property belonging to the Saṅgha or others with the intention to steal, he commits offenses such as Dukkaṭa (depending on the value).

It is not proper to personally plant, cause others to plant, or tend to fruit-bearing or flowering trees in any way for the sake of currying favor with families.

However, for the sake of personal use (by the Saṅgha), planting and other such actions may be performed through making signs, giving hints, using allowable speech (kappiya-vohāra), or using indirect speech (pariyāya).

It has already been stated that providing medical treatment and acting as a messenger (jaṅghapesana) in the affairs of laypeople (results in an offense). Parents and one's own monastery attendants are excepted (it is permissible to perform these for them).
179:
In carrying a message as a messenger, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is committed with every step. Even if one does not take the message, [an offense of wrongdoing is committed] by the one who speaks first. Thus, due to the arising circumstances, these five things—lying, trading, handling [gold and silver, etc.], and so on—are also not allowable for monks.

It is allowable to give [flowers] to parents or other relatives, whether by sending them or taking them oneself. It is allowable to give flowers to those who come to worship objects such as shrines (cetiya). It is not allowable to give them for the purpose of decoration or for the purpose of adorning the body.

Similarly, it is allowable to give fruit to the sick (gilāna), to kings and officials endowed with wealth and retinue, and to those whose provisions have run out, whether the property belongs to oneself or to another.

When distributing fruits and flowers, they should be given to whoever arrives. One who is authorized (sammata) by the Saṅgha should give them. If it is another person, they should give them after asking for permission.

Alternatively, after making an agreement and defining [the portion] in the monastery, they should be given to the sick or others according to that definition. To one who comes to beg, the agreement should be stated, and only the trees should be shown.

Regarding the powder of Sirīsa flowers, grass-knot powder, and so on, and other remaining things, the decision is the same as the method already mentioned. Here, leaves should also be included in the same manner.
