## 39. Description of Entering the Rains Retreat (Vassūpanāyikaniddesa)
There are two types of entering the rains retreat: the earlier (purimikā) and the later (pacchimikā). In that entering of the retreat, the taking up of the residence (ālaya-pariggāha) and the verbal utterance (vacī-bheda) should be understood thus. The verbal utterance (vacī-bheda) is saying: "I enter the rains retreat in this monastery for these three months," or "I enter the rains retreat in this place." The arising of the intention to enter the retreat is called the attachment (ālaya) in this context. If one does not wish to enter the retreat and crosses the boundary of the monastery on the day of entering the retreat, or if a monk knows it is the day to enter the retreat but does not do so, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is committed. A monk whose earlier retreat is broken, or a monk who could not enter the earlier retreat due to an obstacle, must enter the second retreat (pacchimikā). Having entered thus, he must stay for the three months without wandering on tour. For the benefit of parents, for the benefit of the five classes of co-religionists, to seek food and medicine for the sick and their attendants, one may go. [Thinking,] "I will go and inquire after the sick, I will attend to them, I will bring back a dissatisfied co-religionist, I will dispel remorse (kukkucca) regarding the Vinaya, I will clear away wrong views, I will help [someone] rise from a grave offense (garuka-āpatti), etc."—if one wishes to go for the purpose of doing it oneself or having another do it, for dispelling, for seclusion, for rising from an offense, or for making an effort, etc., one is permitted to go for a seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya), whether sent for or not. One may go for the business of the Saṅgha. One may go if invited to listen to the Dhamma, or if sent by teachers, or to see one's teachers.
181:
One should not go [during the retreat] for the purpose of washing requisites such as robes, for reciting and studying the Pali texts, or for the desire to see relatives other than parents or supporting lay donors. If a monk goes to a place not far away with the intention of "returning this very day," but is unable to return before dawn (due to various reasons), such failure to return is permitted (there is no breaking of the retreat or offense).

If sent for by relatives other than parents, or by those who depend on the monk, one is permitted to go (even without a specific reason). However, if invited by laymen or laywomen, one is permitted to go only if they indicate a reason such as wishing to give alms or wishing to listen to the Dhamma.

If there is danger to oneself, or for the sake of the unity of the Saṅgha, there is no offense if the retreat is broken. A monk whose retreat is broken shall not perform the pavarāṇā ceremony.

It is not allowable to enter the rains retreat in the open air, in a hollow tree, in the fork of a tree, or on a couch, under an umbrella, or in a large jar in a cemetery.

A monk without a monastery is also not allowed to enter the retreat. A monk who enters the retreat in a place belonging to boatmen, a caravan of traders, or cowherds, is permitted to perform the pavarāṇā ceremony when the retreat is over.

## 40. Description of Non-distributable Items (Avebhaṅgiyaniddesa)
Non-distributable items (avebhaṅgiya) are:
Parks and park-lands; monasteries and monastery-lands; beds, stools, bolsters, pillows, and other such bedding and seating;
Copper pots, iron pots,
Copper basins, copper jars,
Axes, hatchets, adzes,
Hoes, and chisels.
182:
Creepers, bamboo, grass, leaves, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, clay, wooden articles, and clay articles—these five groups are indivisible (avibhājiya).

An offense of grave guilt (thullaccaya) is committed by a monk who distributes these indivisible items. Even if they have been distributed, they are considered undistributed (they do not belong to individuals but remain the property of the Saṅgha). These items are called heavy property (garubhaṇḍa) and items that are not to be given away (avissajjiya).

Creepers the size of half an arm, bamboo eight finger-breadths in length, grass the size of a handful, even a single leaf, and clay—whether natural or of five colors, or mixed with plaster, resin, etc., the size of a ripe palmyra fruit—[are non-distributable].

Ropes, leather thongs, and so on, which are given to the Saṅgha or which arise on Saṅgha land and are protected, are non-distributable. However, when the work of the Saṅgha or the work of a shrine (cetiya) is completed, [the surplus] may be distributed.

Among iron and copper items, those suitable for monks such as alms-bowls, whether finished or unfinished, and pots or vessels with a capacity of one pāda (five Magadha units), may be distributed.

Among bamboo items, oil tubes, walking sticks, umbrella handles, bamboo slats for umbrella frames, and sticks for hanging sandals may be distributed.
183:
The handle of a permitted small knife, a casket holding one pāda (equivalent to 5 Magadhan māsakas), a lathe, a lathe-cylinder, a collyrium box, a horn, and other such requisites of monks, as well as unfinished carved wooden items and ivory, may be distributed. A small pot made of fine clay holding one pāda, used as a monk's requisite, may also be distributed.

Permissible leather may be distributed. However, sheepskin may not be distributed. Heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa) may be exchanged for other heavy goods or for immovable goods (thāvarabhaṇḍa). Immovable goods may also be exchanged for other immovable goods. Use them after making such an exchange. Creepers and such should be taken through the process of increase (phātikamma). It should be known that other remaining items may not be distributed.

## 41. Pakinnakaniddeso

In explaining miscellaneous matters:
In a place equipped with door-leaves, door-frames, a lower socket, and an upper ring, a monk lying down during the day should close the door that turns by opening and closing.

If a wise man is present, the thought 'This person will guard the door' is also permissible. A monk who lies down in his own area without such closing or such a thought commits a dukkaṭa offense.

A monk who touches the ten kinds of jewels, female figures (figures of female beings), the seven kinds of grain, women's ornaments, musical instruments, or weapons commits a dukkaṭa offense.
184:
A monk who smooths down or combs his hair with oil mixed with wax, oil mixed with water, ivory combs, hand-combs, or bristle combs commits a dukkaṭa offense.

Monks should not sleep together under a single cover or on a single mat; likewise, they should not sleep together on a single couch, nor should they eat together from a single vessel.

One should not chew a tooth-stick (dantakaṭṭha) shorter than four finger-breadths or longer than eight finger-breadths. Unless one is ill, one should not eat garlic.

If one speaks to a person of low or high status using abusive terms such as birth (caste), etc., whether directly or by implying it as if speaking to another, with a desire to joke, one commits a dubbhāsita offense.

One should not keep long fingernails, toenails, hair, or nose hair. One should not polish the twenty nails to make them smooth, nor should one remove hair from private areas.

One should not obstruct the order of seniority in lodgings intended for the Saṅgha or belonging to the Saṅgha. One should not step on the bedding or the monastery without washing one's feet or while one's feet are wet. Even if the feet are well-washed, one should not step on them while wearing sandals.

One should not sit with one's knees wrapped with a determined (adhiṭṭhāna) robe. One should not lean against painted walls and such without a covering cloth. One should not remain without washing after using the toilet when water is available (one must wash).
185: A monk commits a dukkaṭa offense by causing someone to undertake an improper action, by rolling down a stone in jest, by confessing a shared offense (sabhāga āpatti), or by making it known. A monk with a pure mind who fails to fulfill a promise commits a dukkaṭa offense. However, for a monk without a pure mind (with intent to deceive), a pācittiya offense is committed at the very moment of making the promise. One should not climb a tree. If there is a necessity, one may climb to the height of a man. In times of danger, one may climb as much as desired. A monk who travels a long distance without a water filter (parissāvana) commits a dukkaṭa offense. A monk who does not give a water filter when requested during a long journey commits a dukkaṭa offense. Except for reasons of illness, cutting off the male organ results in a thullaccaya offense. Cutting off other limbs or harming oneself results in a dukkaṭa offense. One should not make artistic figures oneself, nor cause others to make them. One should not make a monk rise from his seat while he is eating in a monastery, a forest, or a house. A sick monk is permitted to ride in vehicles yoked with oxen, etc., a palanquin, a hand-cart, or a cloth-litter. A monk commits a dukkaṭa offense by joking about the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, or by enticing the followers of another.
186:
A monk should not expose his body, thigh, or private parts to nuns. He should not splash those nuns with liquid such as muddy water.

A monk who does not accept the instruction (ovāda) requested by nuns, or who does not convey the instruction back, commits a dukkaṭa offense, except for a monk who does not know the method of giving instruction, a sick monk, or a monk about to go on a journey.

One should not teach the Lokāyata text. One should not have grey hairs plucked. One should not eat from a box (used as a bowl-stand). One should not play any kind of game.

One should not wear the upper robe or the lower robe in the manner of laypeople. One should not wear the lower robe tucked up. One should not set fire to a forest.

One should not arrange for interest or profit, nor should one request items from those who are not relatives or who have not invited such requests. One should not give to another person items donated for one's own use. However, one may give it after taking the best portion or after using it for a few days.

When requesting protection by specifying a certain person, whether one knows or does not know that a fine will be imposed, if a fine is imposed, that fine becomes a debt of the monk who requested the protection. In the case of personally causing a fine to be imposed, the offenses such as pārājika should be known according to the value of the fine.
187:
359. While requisites are being stolen, if a monk shouts 'Thief! Thief!' with the intention of causing harm to them, and if the authorities arrest them and impose a fine, the monk must compensate for the amount of the fine; that fine becomes a debt (bhaṇḍāsā) for the monk.

360. If a monk discards food scraps, excrement, rubbish, or urine outside the walls or fences, or on a path used by many people, or in a green area where crops, coconut trees, etc., are planted, without looking, he commits a dukkaṭa offense.

361. Even if associated with merit, one should not cause others to dance, sing, or play music, nor do it oneself, nor watch or listen to such performances performed by others. If someone offers, 'We shall perform an offering with a festival,' it should not be accepted.

362. A monk who goes to see a royal pavilion, a pond, a garden, a house decorated with paintings or sculptures, or a fruit or flower orchard, which are made for the sake of amusement, commits a dukkaṭa offense.

363. One should not obstruct junior monks from their places (should not make them rise from their seats). One should not dry a robe in the sun for a long time. If expelled from the monastery by a teacher or preceptor (upajjhāya), one must beg for forgiveness to be allowed to stay.

364. A monk commits a dukkaṭa offense by insulting another monk behind his back with the seven classes of offenses, or by insulting either a monk or a lay follower (upāsaka) with words other than those related to offenses.

## Pakinnakaniddesa

365. Requisites such as robes donated out of faith should not be diverted or given away improperly (should not be given to laypeople). It is permitted to give them to one's parents; it is not permitted to give them to relatives other than parents.
188:
A robe offered out of faith and devotion should not be diverted (given to another). It is permissible to give it to one's parents. It is not permissible to give it to other relatives besides parents.

A monk who has spent the rains retreat in another monastery and takes a share of robes from a different monastery commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). That share must be returned. If it is lost or worn out, it remains as a debt. If, despite being asked, he does not give it and the owners of the property give up their effort to recover it, the case should be decided according to the value of the property.

One should not enter a village without the upper robe (santaruttara). A healthy monk should not enter a village wearing sandals. One should not carry a mosquito fan or a whisk made of yak-tail hair.

Unless ill, one should not cut hair with scissors. Outside the monastery grounds, one should not carry an umbrella. However, for the sake of protecting the robes or for self-protection, it is permissible to carry an umbrella.

One should not carry a load with a carrying pole on both sides. A carrying pole with a load on one side or in the middle is permissible. Loads carried on the head, shoulder, waist, or suspended by hand are permissible.

If one accuses a monk who has not yet given permission of an offense, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Similarly, it is an offense of wrongdoing to ask for permission to accuse a pure monk without cause.

One should not use a bed-frame leg that exceeds eight finger-breadths of a regular person. One should not use a bed with high legs.
189:
One should not use a bed-frame leg exceeding eight finger-breadths of a regular person; nor should one use a bed with legs exceeding eight finger-breadths of the Buddha.

If one undertakes and practices the observances of sectarians, such as the vow of silence, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Likewise, if a monk who was formerly a barber keeps barber's tools as his own, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

It is allowable to request any kind of manual labor (hatthakamma) and to accept the requisites obtained following that request. Even without requesting manual labor from someone who is idle, it is allowable to have the work done, or to have materials like grass or wood that belong to others (or are ownerless) carried.

If guards or others give property belonging to laypeople, it is permissible to take as much as is given. However, regarding property belonging to the Saṅgha or a Cetiya, it is permissible to take only according to the portion designated for those guards.

An offense may be committed through two means: body and speech, or through the six origins (samuṭṭhāna). An offense may also be committed due to shamelessness, ignorance, remorse (kukkucca), or lack of mindfulness; or by perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, or what is allowable as unallowable.

Due to shamelessness or ignorance, one may conceal an offense through body or speech. Rehabilitation from an offense occurs through four means: change of gender (liṅga), the Saṅgha, a group (gaṇa), or an individual.

Regarding the two requisites of robes and alms-food, one should not use indirect talk (parikathā), hinting (obhāsa), or direct intimation (viññatti). Regarding the third requisite, lodgings, only direct intimation is not allowed. Regarding the remaining requisite, medicine, all three—indirect talk, hinting, and intimation—are permissible.

Giving property to the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika) to be taken only after one's death is not valid. That property belongs only to the Saṅgha. However, in the case of laypeople, giving property to be taken after death is valid.

If a monk or a novice passes away in a nunnery, only the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha is entitled to inherit his property. This same rule applies to the property of deceased nuns (bhikkhunīs) and others.

Regarding property given through a messenger with the instruction, "Take this item and give it to such-and-such a person"...
190:
If a monk or a novice passes away in a nunnery, only the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha is entitled to inherit his property. This same rule applies to the property of deceased nuns (bhikkhunīs) and others.

Property given with the words, "Take this object and give it to that person," belongs to the original owner. Property given with the words, "I give this object to that person," belongs to the recipient. Knowing this procedure, one may take it on trust (vissāsagāha) or by determining it as the robe of a deceased person (matakacīvara).

Among iron and bronze items, all items are allowable except weapons. Among wooden items, all wooden items are allowable except wooden alms-bowls, sandals, thrones, and couches/benches. Among clay items, all clay items are allowable except foot-scrubbers in the shape of a lotus and small huts made by potters.

## 42. Exposition of Confession (Desanāniddesa)

Confession (desanā) means:
Giving up the status of a monk is the confession of a pārājika offense.
Emerging from an offense according to the stated method is the confession of a grave offense (garukāpatti).

Sitting in a squatting position, with hands raised in salutation (añjali), one should confess offenses such as thullaccaya in the presence of another monk as follows:
191:
"Venerable Sir, I have fallen into a single thullaccaya offense; I confess it in your presence." When the confessing monk says, "Friend, do you see that offense?" he should reply, "Yes, Venerable Sir, I see it." When the monk says again, "Friend, you should practice restraint in the future," he should say, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I shall practice restraint." "Venerable Sir, I have fallen into two thullaccaya offenses... Venerable Sir, I have fallen into many thullaccaya offenses; I confess them in your presence."

In the case of forfeiture (nissaggiya) offenses: "Venerable Sir, this robe of mine, having exceeded ten days, is to be forfeited. I forfeit this robe to the Venerable One." In the case of an offense that does not lead to confession, or a non-offense (anāpatti) that has already been confessed, monks of different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) staying outside the boundary (sīmā) should not declare it to many monks, as it is performed mentally by a group of four or five. 

## 43. Explanation of Giving Consent (Chandadānaniddesa)
Regarding the giving of consent (chanda) and so on: After sounding the large drum, conch, gong, metal block, or bell, when the Saṅgha has assembled in accordance with the act (kamma), one should have the consent (chanda), purity (pārisuddhi), or invitation (pavāraṇā) conveyed. A wise monk, skilled in the Vinaya, should approach another monk, sit in a squatting position, raise his joined palms, and give his consent. 

(a) He should say: "I give my consent, please convey my consent, please announce my consent to the Saṅgha."
(b) When giving purity, he should say: "I give my purity, please convey my purity, please announce my purity to the Saṅgha."

By giving purity, he fulfills the Uposatha act for both the Saṅgha and himself. However, it prevents other Saṅgha acts apart from the Uposatha. By giving consent, he fulfills both acts (Uposatha and other acts) for the Saṅgha, but not for himself. Therefore, a monk giving consent should also give his purity. A single monk can convey the consent and purity of many monks. However, it should not be conveyed through successive stages. Consent and purity conveyed through successive stages do not reach the Saṅgha.
199:
A single monk can carry the consent and purity of many monks. However, it should not be carried in a succession. Consent and purity carried in a succession do not reach the Sangha.

After performing all the preliminary etiquettes (upacāra), one should give the invitation (pavāraṇā) in this way: "I give my pavāraṇā, please carry my pavāraṇā, please report my pavāraṇā to the Sangha, please invite on my behalf."

Then, that monk who has brought it, upon reaching the Sangha, should report and then invite the Sangha thus: "Venerable Sirs, the monk named so-and-so invites the Sangha [to speak] regarding what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the Sangha speak to him out of compassion. Seeing the fault, he will rectify it."

If the monk who is carrying the purity, consent, or pavāraṇā, before reaching the Sangha, disrobes, dies, or admits to becoming a novice, etc., it is not considered "carried." If such an event occurs after the carrier has reached the Sangha, it is considered "carried."

If, after reaching the Sangha, he fails to report due to forgetfulness or sleep, there is no offense. For a monk who intentionally does not report while knowing, there is a Dukkaṭa offense.

## 44. Explanation of Uposatha (Uposatha-niddesa)

Regarding Uposatha—
There are two types by day: the 14th day Uposatha (cātuddasī) and the 15th day Uposatha (pannarasī). There are three types by the method of performance: Suttuddesa Uposatha, Adhiṭṭhāna Uposatha, and Pārisuddhi Uposatha.

Suttuddesa Uposatha is for the Sangha only. Adhiṭṭhāna Uposatha is for a single individual only. For a group (gaṇa) of two or three remaining monks, it is Pārisuddhi Uposatha.

When the five preliminary duties (pubbakicca), four preliminary rituals (pubbakaraṇa), and the act at the appropriate time (pattakalla) are fulfilled, the Sangha should recite the Pātimokkha Sutta. That Suttuddesa Uposatha is explained in five ways.

Abridging the recitation without the ten dangers is specifically prohibited. However, because it is said, "In these five recitations, if one knows two or three recitations clearly by heart, the elder is the master," abridging is allowable even if no danger occurs.

If an equal number of monks or a few monks arrive while the recitation is in progress, what has been recited is well-recited; the rest should be listened to.
201:
If the Pātimokkha has just been recited, or if the whole Sangha or some of the Sangha have already risen and left, the Pārisuddhi Uposatha should be performed in the presence of those monks. If the monks who arrive later are more numerous than the original Sangha, the preliminary duties should be performed in all variations (vikap), and the Pātimokkha should be recited again.

If it is the 15th day Uposatha for the resident monks (āvāsika) and the 14th day Uposatha for the guest monks (āgantuka), if the guests are equal in number to the residents, they should follow the view of the residents who were there first. If the guests are more numerous, the residents who were there first should follow the view of those guests. This same method applies to the remaining cases.

If it is the 1st day of the waning moon for the resident monks and the Uposatha day for the guest monks, if the guests are equal to or fewer than the residents, the resident monks at the original place may give physical harmony (kāya-sāmaggi) as much as they wish.

If they do not give harmony, the guest monks should go outside the boundary (sīmā) and perform the Uposatha. If the guests are more numerous, even if the residents do not wish to give harmony, they should give it, or they should go outside the boundary.

The same method applies when it is the 1st day of the waning moon for the guest monks. The Pātimokkha Pali should be recited so that all can hear; for a monk who intentionally recites so that it cannot be heard, there is a Dukkaṭa offense.

A monk who is healthy but does not perform sweeping, lighting lamps, or arranging water and seats when ordered by a Great Elder (Mahāthera) likewise incurs a Dukkaṭa offense.
202:
Having swept the place, lit the lamps, and prepared the drinking water, usable water, and seats, the Uposatha for three monks should be performed by making the announcement (gaṇa-ñatti) in the following manner: “Venerable sirs, may you listen to my words. Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha. If it is suitable for the venerable sirs, let us perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha among one another.” (This is the motion.)

Placing the robe over the left shoulder, sitting in a squatting position, and raising the joined palms, the elder should speak to the juniors: “Friends, I am pure from offenses; hold me as one who is pure.” This should be spoken three times.

Having completed the preliminary efforts, the junior should also speak to those two monks: “Venerable sirs, I am pure from offenses; hold me as one who is pure.” This should be spoken three times.

When there are two monks, the elder, having performed the necessary duties, should say to the junior: “Friend, I am pure from offenses; hold me as one who is pure.” This should be said three times.

The junior should also say to the elder: “Venerable sir, I am pure from offenses; hold me as one who is pure.” This should be spoken three times.
203:
A single monk, having completed all necessary preliminary duties, should resolve: “Today is my fifteenth-day Uposatha” or “Today is my fourteenth-day Uposatha,” saying “I resolve.” If he does not resolve, he commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

In whatever monastery four, three, or two monks reside, if they perform their respective Uposatha by merely conveying the purity (pārisuddhi) of each individual monk, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) would be incurred.

In a divided Sangha or a united Sangha, if one performs the Uposatha perceiving it as “divided” or with doubt, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is committed by the Sangha. If it is done with the intention of causing a schism, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is committed. In a divided or united Sangha, if one performs it perceiving it as “united,” there is no offense.

A suspended (ukkhitta) person, a layperson, the four remaining types of co-religionists, one who has committed a pārājika offense, an excluded (abhabba) person, and one who has given up the training should not be present in the sitting assembly when the Pātimokkha is recited. Likewise, the Pātimokkha should not be recited by a Sangha that has a common offense (sabhāgāpatti) or with a withheld consent (chanda).

It is not proper to perform the Uposatha without confessing a committed offense, without clarifying a doubtful offense, or on a day that is not an Uposatha day.

One should not leave a monastery where the Uposatha is regularly held on that Uposatha day, except for a danger or for Sangha business, or to resolve a boundary (sīmā). One should not even go to the ordination hall (sīmā) for the purpose of performing the Uposatha by resolution (adhiṭṭhāna).

## 45. Explanation of Pavāraṇā

Pavāraṇā is as follows: there is the mutual invitation of two, three, or four monks; the resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) of a single monk; and the Sangha Pavāraṇā of the remaining five or more monks. Having performed the preliminary duties (pubbakicca) and preliminary obligations (pubbakaraṇa), and when the proper time has arrived, the Sangha should perform the Pavāraṇā by making the motion (ñatti) as follows: “Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to my words. Today is the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā. If it is suitable for the Sangha, let the Sangha perform Pavāraṇā.” (This is the motion.)

Placing the robe over the left shoulder, sitting in a squatting position, and raising the joined palms, the elder should speak to the Sangha: “Friends, I invite the Sangha by what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable sirs speak to me out of compassion. Seeing the fault, I shall remedy it. For the second time... for the third time, friends, I invite the Sangha by what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable sirs speak to me out of compassion. Seeing the fault, I shall remedy it.” This should be spoken.

While the elders are performing Pavāraṇā, the junior monk should remain in a squatting position. He should remain squatting until he himself has completed the Pavāraṇā. The junior monk, having completed the preliminary actions, should speak to the Sangha.
205:
“Venerable sirs, I invite the Sangha by what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable sirs speak to me out of compassion. I shall remedy the fault when I see it. For the second time... for the third time, venerable sirs, I invite the Sangha by what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable sirs speak to me out of compassion. I shall remedy the fault when I see it.” (This should be requested.)

Because the night has passed due to giving, Dhamma discussion, or disputes, or if there is no opportunity for the three-fold invitation (tevācika-pavāraṇā), or if there are the ten kinds of dangers, the Pavāraṇā should be performed by reciting the motion (ñatti) appropriately:

“Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to my words. Because of people giving, two monks discussing the Dhamma, or people engaging in disputes, the night has mostly passed. If the Sangha performs the three-fold invitation (tevācika-pavāraṇā), the night will turn into dawn before the Sangha has finished the Pavāraṇā. This is the danger from kings, this is the danger from thieves, this is the danger from fire, this is the danger from water, this is the danger from humans, this is the danger from non-humans, this is the danger from beasts,”
206:
This is a danger from creatures such as snakes, scorpions, and gadflies; this is a danger to life; this is a danger to the holy life. If the Saṅgha performs the invitation (Pavāraṇā) three times (tevācika-pavāraṇā), the Saṅgha will remain without having performed the Pavāraṇā, and then this danger to the holy life will occur. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should perform the invitation twice, or once, or together with those of equal seniority.

One should perform the invitation in accordance with the established motion (ñatti). If those of equal seniority or others arrive, one should apply (the methods mentioned in the Uposatha section) to this Pavāraṇā.

In this way, groups of three or four monks should also perform the invitation after reciting the motion: “Venerables, please listen to me. Today is the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā. If it is suitable for the venerables, let us invite one another.” (This should be recited and performed).

Placing the robe over the left shoulder, sitting in a crouching position, the elder (thera) should raise his hands in reverent salutation (añjali) and address them thus:

“Friends, I invite the venerables [to point out my faults] based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerables speak to me out of compassion; seeing the fault, I shall make amends. For the second time... For the third time, I...”
207:
“...friends, I invite the venerables based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerables speak to me out of compassion; seeing the fault, I shall make amends.”

The junior monk (nava) should also say: “Venerable Sir, I invite the venerables based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerables speak to me out of compassion; seeing the fault, I shall make amends. For the second time... [pe]... For the third time, Venerable Sir, I invite the venerables based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerables speak to me out of compassion; seeing the fault, I shall make amends.”

When there are two monks, the elder should perform the preliminary duties and then address the junior monk thus: “Friend, I invite the venerable based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable speak to me out of compassion; seeing the fault, I shall make amends. For the second time... [pe]... For the third time, friend, I invite the venerable based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable speak to me out of compassion; seeing the fault, I shall make amends.”

The junior monk should also say: “Venerable Sir, I invite the venerable based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable speak to me out of compassion...”
208:
“...seeing the fault, I shall make amends. For the second time... [pe]... For the third time, Venerable Sir, I invite the venerable based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable speak to me out of compassion; seeing the fault, I shall make amends.”

Having completed all necessary preliminary duties, a single monk should make a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) thus: “I determine: Today is my fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā,” or “Today is my fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā.”

In whichever monastery five, four, three, or two monks reside, if they bring the Pavāraṇā of each individual and others perform those respective Pavāraṇās, there shall be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The remaining verses have been stated in the Uposatha section; those verses should be applied here as well.

When the Saṅgha has completed the Pavāraṇā, a monk who has broken the rains-retreat (vassa), or one who did not enter the retreat, or one who has not yet completed the retreat, should perform the Uposatha of Purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha).
209:
On the full moon day of Kattika, which marks the end of the four months of rain, if the Saṅgha has performed the Uposatha and the monks who stayed for the later rains-retreat are few in number, they should perform the Pavāraṇā.

## 46. Saṃvara-niddesa (Exposition on Restraint)
Restraint (Saṃvara) means:
One should prevent the arising of unwholesome states such as covetousness and distress (abhijjhā-domanassa) in the six sense objects such as forms and sounds, through the six sense faculties such as the eye and the ear.

One should subdue one's own mind, just as one subdues a difficult ox that is prone to eating crops.
Being mindful and clearly comprehending, one should practice in all postures.

## 47. Suddhi-niddesa (Exposition on Purity)
Purity (Suddhi) means:
By way of confession (desanā), restraint (saṃvara), seeking (eṭṭhi), and reflection (paccavekkhaṇa),
Purity is of four kinds. The virtue known as restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla),
Is called purity through confession (desanā-suddhi) because it is purified by the act of confessing.
210:
Because of the restraint through mental determination, “I will not do this again,”
Restraint of the sense faculties is said to be purified; this purification is called purity through restraint (saṃvara-suddhi).

In the seeking of a monk who, having abandoned improper search, generates requisites righteously,
It is called purity through seeking (eṭṭhi-suddhi) because it is pure; this is the virtue based on livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla).

One uses the robe after reflecting with wise consideration;
Purification through such reflection as stated in the teachings,
Is called purity through reflection (paccavekkhaṇa-suddhi); this is the virtue based on requisites (paccaya-sannissita-sīla).

## 48. Santosa-niddesa (Exposition on Contentment)
Contentment (Santosa) means:
Being content with little, with what is blameless, and with what is easily obtained,
Being one who knows moderation and is easy to support, one should practice with respect for the True Dhamma.

Without grieving over the past and without longing for the future,
One who sustains oneself with the present is called one who is content.

## 49. Caturārakkha-niddesa (Exposition on the Four Protections)
The four protections are:
Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati), Loving-kindness (Mettā), Impurity (Asubha), and Recollection of Death (Maraṇassati).

He is the Worthy One (Arahaṃ) because He is far from defilements, etc.,
Or He is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) because He has rightly realized all things by Himself;
That which is the repeated recollection [of these qualities],
Upon the ninefold qualities of the Blessed One, is called the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati).
211:
In the assembly of the Saṅgha staying within the access boundary (upacāra-sīmā), and in the deities staying within the access boundary,
in the ruling people in the village where alms are collected, and starting from the people in that village.
"May all beings be happy, may they be free from enmity," and so forth,

By way of color, shape, location, direction, and delimitation,

212:
Mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) should be developed by considering death as being like an executioner standing nearby; by the failure of all successes; by comparing the death of others to oneself; likewise, by the body being subject to many dangers; by the fragility of life; by the fact that the time of death is not fixed; and by the limitation of the life span.

## 50. Explanation of Insight (Vipassanāniddesa)
Regarding insight (vipassanā): Having discerned mind and matter (nāmarūpa), and then discerning the causes of that mind and matter, one applies the three characteristics to formations (saṅkhāra), contemplating them repeatedly: as impermanent (anicca) because they do not exist after having come to be; as suffering (dukkha) because of the oppression of rise and fall; and as non-self (anatta) because they do not follow one's will. By doing so, one may gradually reach the destruction of all fetters (saṃyojana).

## Concluding Words (Nigamanakathā)
The duties of a monk, namely the training in higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā), have been set forth in this Khuddasikkhā. Of that Venerable One whose great fame and reputation circulate through the world, and who, like the gentle breeze that blows constantly, is ever without fatigue...
213: This [Khuddasikkhā] was composed by the Elder named Dhammasirī, who was like a banner of the island of Tambapaṇṇi and was praised by those learned in the Dhamma and Vinaya. To this extent, this Khuddasikkhā, consisting of approximately five hundred verses in length, has reached its conclusion. The Khuddasikkhā is finished.
